result: Internal consistency of SCRs at both time points (T0 and T1) was satisfactory for CS+, CS−, and US responses (ranging from 0.54 to 0.94), but lower for CS discrimination (ranging from −0.01 to 0.60).
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 present internal consistency data from Figure 1 showing satisfactory reliability for individual stimulus responses but lower reliability for difference scores (CS discrimination). The data are clearly presented with confidence intervals and are consistent with established psychometric principles that difference scores tend to have lower reliability.

result: Log-transformation did not impact internal consistency, but log-transformation combined with range correction largely reduced internal consistency.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 report effects of data transformations on internal consistency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The findings are clearly stated and supported by the supplementary data, though the mechanism for why range correction reduces reliability is not fully explained.

result: Longitudinal individual-level reliability (ICCs) was limited across SCRs (0.03-0.61), fear ratings (−0.19 to 0.70), and BOLD fMRI (≤0.17 for whole brain, ≤0.001 for individual ROIs).
evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C69-C71 present ICC data from Figure 1 and Supplementary files showing limited individual-level longitudinal reliability across all outcome measures. The data are comprehensive and appropriately analyzed using established ICC methods, though interpretation is complicated by lack of field-specific benchmarks.

result: Data transformation effects on ICCs varied: log-transformation and range correction increased reliability for some specifications but decreased it for others; including more trials increased ICCs during acquisition and extinction but decreased them during reinstatement-test.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 describe how different data processing choices affected reliability estimates (Figure 1—figure supplements 2-8). The findings are well-documented across multiple supplementary figures, though the inconsistent effects across phases suggest complex interactions that may require further investigation.

result: For SCRs, within-subject similarity was not significantly different from between-subject similarity for most data specifications, with exceptions for US responses during acquisition (t(70)=2.54, p=0.013) and CS− responses during extinction (t(31)=2.05, p=0.049).
evaluation: Claims C72-C79 present similarity analyses from Figure 2 with appropriate statistical tests. The finding that individual SCR patterns are not more similar to themselves over time than to other individuals is striking and well-supported, though the wide variance in within-subject similarity suggests substantial individual differences.

result: For BOLD fMRI, within-subject similarity was significantly higher than between-subject similarity for acquisition training (p<0.001 for whole brain and most ROIs) but not for extinction training (all p's>0.306).
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 present BOLD fMRI similarity analyses from Figure 3 and Supplementary file 6. The contrast between acquisition and extinction is well-documented and statistically significant, suggesting phase-specific differences in reliability that warrant further investigation.

result: Individual-level BOLD activation overlap was low, with Jaccard coefficients of 7.60% for acquisition and 0.70% for extinction, with large interindividual variability (0-39.65% for acquisition).
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 present overlap analyses from Table 2A showing very limited spatial consistency of individual activation patterns over time. The large range of individual values (C85) is particularly informative, though the reasons for this variability are not explored.

result: Longitudinal group-level reliability was robust for both SCRs (40.66-75.67% explained variance for acquisition) and BOLD fMRI (62.00% whole brain overlap for acquisition), but much lower for extinction training.
evaluation: Claims C130-C131, C142-C145 present group-level reliability data from Figure 4 and Table 2B. The stark contrast between robust group-level and limited individual-level reliability is well-documented and represents a key finding, though the mechanisms underlying this discrepancy require further investigation.

result: For SCRs, acquisition training performance predicted fear recall for most data specifications, but predictions of extinction end-point performance and reinstatement-test performance were largely non-significant regardless of data transformation.
evaluation: Claims C93-C97 present cross-phase prediction analyses from Figure 5A. The selective predictability (strong for fear recall, absent for later phases) is well-documented across multiple data specifications, though the underlying mechanisms are not fully explained.

result: For fear ratings, acquisition training performance predicted responding at fear recall, extinction training, and reinstatement-test, but predictions of post-extinction performance were mostly non-significant.
evaluation: Claims C98-C109 present cross-phase prediction analyses for fear ratings from Figure 5B. The pattern differs from SCRs in showing more consistent cross-phase predictions, which is well-documented though the reasons for measure-specific differences are not fully explored.

result: For BOLD fMRI, nearly all associations between acquisition and extinction were positive but weak (standardized betas mostly <0.3), with the exception of CS+ associations in the dACC.
evaluation: Claims C112-C113 present BOLD fMRI cross-phase predictions from Figure 6. The weak associations are clearly documented, though the functional significance of these weak correlations and the exception in dACC warrant further investigation.

result: Cross-phase prediction strength varied by data transformation: standardized betas were significantly higher for log-transformed and range-corrected SCRs compared to raw or log-transformed data, and higher for non-ranked compared to ranked SCRs.
evaluation: Claims C114-C118 present statistical comparisons of prediction strength across data specifications with appropriate t-tests and effect sizes. The findings highlight the importance of data processing choices, though optimal transformation strategies remain unclear.

result: Standardized betas for CS discrimination were significantly lower than for CS+ and CS− for both SCRs and BOLD fMRI, but for ratings, CS discrimination betas were higher than CS− and comparable to CS+.
evaluation: Claims C119-C124 present systematic comparisons across stimulus types with appropriate statistical tests. The measure-specific patterns are well-documented and consistent with psychometric principles about difference scores, though mechanistic explanations are limited.

result: Standardized betas were larger for CS+ than CS− across all outcome measures (SCRs: t(65)=3.79, p<0.001; ratings: t(21)=3.12, p=0.005; BOLD fMRI: t(11)=4.34, p=0.001).
evaluation: Claims C125-C127 present consistent findings across all three outcome measures with appropriate statistical tests and effect sizes. The consistency across measures strengthens confidence in this finding.

result: Predictions of fear recall were significantly stronger than predictions of reinstatement-test for both SCRs (t(124)=4.35, p<0.001, d=0.86) and fear ratings (t(40)=5.15, p<0.001, d=1.76).
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 present comparisons between prediction strengths for different phases with appropriate statistical tests and large effect sizes. The findings are robust and consistent across measures.

result: Longitudinal individual-level reliability was more limited across outcome measures and data specifications, particularly during extinction training, as assessed by ICCs and BOLD activation overlap.
evaluation: Claims C132-C133 summarize the overall pattern of limited individual-level reliability from Figures 1C-F and Table 2A. This is a key integrative finding supported by multiple analyses, though the phase-specific differences (particularly for extinction) require further mechanistic investigation.

result: The longitudinal individual-level reliability findings are consistent with previous fear conditioning studies reporting comparable figures across outcome measures and experimental phases.
evaluation: Claim C134 contextualizes the current findings within prior literature (Cooper et al., 2022b; Fredrikson et al., 1993; Ridderbusch et al., 2021; Torrents-Rodas et al., 2014; Zeidan et al., 2012). The consistency across studies strengthens confidence in the findings, though direct quantitative comparisons are limited by methodological differences.

result: SCRs of individuals at T0 were not more similar to their own responses at T1 than to others, but for BOLD fMRI, individual acquisition patterns at T0 were more similar to their own patterns at T1 than to others' patterns (not true for extinction).
evaluation: Claims C135-C137 present complementary similarity analyses from Figures 2-3. The measure-specific differences (SCR vs. BOLD fMRI) are well-documented and represent an important methodological insight, though the underlying reasons for these differences are speculative.

result: BOLD fMRI might be more sensitive to detect individual-level response similarity than SCRs, possibly due to dependence on spatial (voxel-by-voxel) rather than temporal (trial-by-trial) patterns.
evaluation: Claim C138 offers a speculative explanation for the observed differences between SCR and BOLD fMRI similarity. While the speculation is reasonable, it lacks direct empirical support and alternative explanations (e.g., different signal-to-noise characteristics, different sources of variability) are not systematically evaluated.

result: Longitudinal individual-level reliability was slightly higher for log-transformed and range-corrected SCRs for most specifications, but increasing the number of trials did not generally improve reliability, suggesting relative stability across data transformations and paradigm specifications.
evaluation: Claims C139-C141 present systematic analyses of how data processing affects reliability (Figure 1—figure supplements 3-8). The finding that more trials don't improve reliability contrasts with other paradigms and is well-documented, though the reasons for this paradigm-specific pattern require further investigation.

result: Higher reliability during acquisition compared to extinction training has been described in the literature and may be explained by floor effects due to lower CS discrimination during extinction, which might have lowered internal consistency and longitudinal reliability.
evaluation: Claims C146-C148 integrate current findings with prior literature and offer a plausible explanation (floor effects). The pattern is well-documented (Fredrikson et al., 1993; Zeidan et al., 2012), though the floor effect explanation, while reasonable, is not directly tested.

result: The discrepancy between robust group-level and limited individual-level longitudinal reliability has been reported for other experimental paradigms, and the current results add fear conditioning to this list, with important implications since group-level findings may not represent any individual.
evaluation: Claims C149-C151 contextualize the findings within broader methodological literature (Fröhner et al., 2019; Hedge et al., 2018; Fisher et al., 2018). The integration is appropriate and the implications are clearly stated, representing an important contribution to understanding measurement properties in experimental neuroscience.

result: Higher responses in previous phases were generally modestly associated with higher responses in subsequent phases across all outcome measures, but a remarkable amount of predictions were non-significant, particularly for CS discrimination in SCRs and BOLD fMRI.
evaluation: Claims C152-C153 summarize the cross-phase prediction findings from Figures 5-6. The pattern of selective predictability is well-documented across multiple measures and specifications, representing a key finding about the limits of cross-phase prediction.

result: The non-significant predictions for CS discrimination may be explained by difference scores being generally less reliable due to subtraction of meaningful variance, and floor effects at the end of extinction where CS discrimination is low.
evaluation: Claims C154-C155 offer explanations for the limited predictability of CS discrimination, supported by psychometric literature (Infantolino et al., 2018; Lynam et al., 2006; Moriarity and Alloy, 2021; Thomas and Zumbo, 2012). The explanations are plausible and well-grounded in measurement theory, though not directly tested in the current data.

result: Mixed findings in the literature regarding cross-phase prediction (independence in experimental studies vs. dependence in clinical samples) might point toward a translational gap, and the strength of associations may depend on the specific outcome measure and its specifications.
evaluation: Claims C156-C157 offer speculative interpretations of mixed literature findings. While the speculation is reasonable and the current data show measure-specific effects, the translational gap hypothesis is not directly tested and alternative explanations (e.g., methodological differences, sample characteristics) are not systematically evaluated.

result: Individual differences in consolidation efficacy may underlie differences in cross-phase predictability, as memory strength is determined by both initial acquisition and consolidation, and the 24-hour delay between phases likely allows consolidation differences to impact test performance.
evaluation: Claims C158-C161 propose consolidation as a mechanism for limited cross-phase prediction. While the reasoning is plausible and grounded in memory literature (Lonsdorf et al., 2019b), consolidation was not directly measured and alternative explanations are not systematically evaluated. This remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing.

result: Together with robust internal consistency, the pattern of findings suggests that individual-level predictions at short intervals are plausible but might be more problematic for longer time periods.
evaluation: Claim C162 integrates internal consistency findings (Figure 1) with longitudinal reliability data to draw conclusions about temporal limits of prediction. The inference is well-supported by the data pattern, though the specific time threshold for reliable prediction is not precisely defined.

result: The reported reliability values may point toward good rather than limited reliability, as interpretation is guided by benchmarks from psychometric work on trait self-report measures, and the upper bound of maximally observable reliability may differ for experimental data which inherently has more noise.
evaluation: Claims C163-C164 provide important critical reflection on the interpretation of reliability values. The point about inappropriate benchmarks is well-taken and represents an important methodological contribution, though the lack of field-specific benchmarks remains a limitation.

result: Predictions in fear conditioning paradigms appear not to be meaningful for longer periods (~6 months), and a key contribution is highlighting the need to pay more attention to measurement properties in translational research and fear conditioning research specifically.
evaluation: Claims C165-C166 draw conclusions about the temporal limits of prediction and the broader implications for the field. The conclusions are well-supported by the data, though the specific time threshold (6 months) is based on a single interval and may not generalize to other intervals.

result: It remains an open question what 'good reliability' in experimental neuroscientific work actually means.
evaluation: Claim C167 acknowledges a fundamental limitation in interpreting reliability in experimental contexts (Parsons et al., 2019). This represents an important methodological point that contextualizes the entire study's findings.

result: Limited individual-level reliability might indicate the paradigm (100% reinforcement rate) is better suited for group effects than individual differences due to limited between-subject variance, but high reliability appears possible in principle given the robust internal consistency of SCRs.
evaluation: Claims C168-C169 offer competing interpretations of the limited individual-level reliability. While both are plausible, they are somewhat contradictory and neither is definitively supported. The robust internal consistency (C169) argues against excessive noise, but doesn't fully explain the limited longitudinal reliability.

result: Limited individual-level but robust group-level reliability might be partly due to different averaging procedures which impact error variance, as group-level data are based on highly aggregated data resulting in reduced error variance.
evaluation: Claims C170-C171 offer a statistical explanation for the group vs. individual reliability discrepancy, supported by Kennedy et al., 2021. The explanation is mathematically sound and represents an important methodological insight, though it doesn't fully account for the magnitude of the observed differences.

result: Different operationalizations of the same measurement might have different reliabilities, as amygdala habituation is more reliable than average activation, and more advanced analytical approaches have been suggested to have better reliability than traditional approaches.
evaluation: Claims C172-C174 discuss how measurement operationalization affects reliability, supported by multiple citations (Plichta et al., 2014; Månsson et al., 2021; Kragel et al., 2021; Marek et al., 2020; Noble et al., 2021; Visser et al., 2021). This represents an important direction for future work, though these alternative approaches were not tested in the current study.

result: Methodological advances in measurement quality and tools may ultimately result in better reliability estimates.
evaluation: Claim C175 discusses potential methodological improvements (Kong et al., 2021; Feilong et al., 2021; DeYoung et al., 2022). While speculative regarding the current data, this represents a reasonable direction for future research.

result: Higher reliability is observed at short test-retest intervals, longer intervals are more susceptible to true changes due to environmental influences, most fMRI reliability studies used shorter intervals (<6 months), and the current results should be conceptualized as longitudinal stability rather than genuine test-retest reliability.
evaluation: Claims C176-C179 contextualize the 6-month interval within the broader reliability literature (Noble et al., 2021; Werner et al., 2022; Specht et al., 2011; Vaidya et al., 2002; Elliott et al., 2020). The distinction between stability and reliability is important and well-justified, representing a key interpretive point.

result: Satisfactory internal consistency speaks against excessive noisiness inherent to the measures, suggesting a true change of the measurand during the retest interval and potentially stronger state than trait dependency.
evaluation: Claims C180-C181 use internal consistency findings to argue for state vs. trait interpretation. The logic is sound and represents an important insight about the nature of fear conditioning measures, though direct evidence for state changes is not provided.

result: Fear conditioning has been highlighted as promising for clinical translation, but the results suggest measurement reliability may allow individual-level predictions for very short but not longer time intervals (6 months), while robust group-level reliability appears to allow group-level predictions over longer intervals.
evaluation: Claims C182-C184 integrate the findings to draw conclusions about translational potential. The conclusions are well-supported by the data and represent a major contribution to understanding the limits and possibilities of fear conditioning research for clinical translation.

result: A potential solution might be using homogenous latent subgroups characterized by similar response profiles to exploit the fact that reliability appears higher for more homogenous samples.
evaluation: Claims C185-C186 propose a methodological solution based on subgroup analysis (Galatzer-Levy et al., 2013a; Gulliksen, 1950). While the proposal is reasonable and grounded in measurement theory, it was not tested in the current data and remains speculative.

result: The work highlights the value of using multiple, more nuanced measures of reliability beyond traditional ICCs (similarity, overlap), and shows no increase in reliability with increasing number of trials in an experiment with a learning component.
evaluation: Claims C187-C188 summarize key methodological contributions. The use of multiple reliability measures is well-demonstrated throughout the paper, and the finding about trial number is clearly documented in Figure 1—figure supplements 3-8, representing important methodological insights.

result: Reliability is a property of a measure that is not fixed and may vary depending on task specifications and samples, and is not a fixed property of the task itself.
evaluation: Claims C189-C190 emphasize the context-dependent nature of reliability (Parsons, 2020). This represents an important conceptual point that is well-supported by the observed variability across specifications in the current study.

result: We may need to develop paradigms and data processing pipelines explicitly tailored to individual difference research or experimental research questions, as measurement reliability has major consequences on effect sizes and statistical power.
evaluation: Claims C191-C192 propose a major shift in research approach based on the findings (Parsons, 2020; Elliott et al., 2020). The proposal is well-justified by the data showing different reliability at group vs. individual levels, representing an important recommendation for the field.

result: Multiverse-type investigations that systematically scrutinize the impact of alternative processing and analytical decisions may be helpful to achieve the aim of developing paradigms tailored to specific research questions.
evaluation: Claim C193 proposes multiverse approaches as a methodological solution (Parsons, 2020; Steegen et al., 2016; Kuhn et al., 2022; Lonsdorf et al., 2022; Sjouwerman et al., 2022). The current study demonstrates this approach and shows its value, representing both a methodological contribution and a recommendation for future work.

result: Work on measurement questions should be included in cognitive-experimental work as standard practice and can be explored cost-effectively in existing data, and devoting resources to measurement optimization is a valuable investment for improved mental health.
evaluation: Claims C194-C195 make recommendations for research practice (Parsons, 2020; Moriarity and Alloy, 2021). The recommendations are well-justified by the findings and represent important guidance for the field, though implementation challenges are not discussed.
